name: Kimaghama
confidence_why: Geurtjens 1933 puts main stress on the last syllable in a single note that covers the wordlists of six neighbouring languages at once, whereas Drabbe 1949, the only linguist who worked on Kimaghama itself, marks stress mostly on the first syllable in his wordlist but expressly declines to say what kind of stress the language has, and Voorhoeve 1975 merely reads Drabbe's accent marks as unpredictable, so no one has actually analysed Kimaghama stress and any rule is a guess.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked the two copies we hold by rendering the stated pages (no new downloads; nothing added to. (1), p. 409 = printed p. 365, sect. 2.6.2.2.4.1 'Kimaghama': the quote is there verbatim, immediately after the tentative phoneme inventory 'on the basis of Drabbe's notes': 'Suprasegmentals: stress, the occurrence of which seems unpredictable. (Stress is therefore potentially phonemic, but no cases of phonemic stress contrast have been recorded.)' Sect. 2.6.2.2.4.2 Riantana, same page: 'Suprasegmentals: as in Kimaghama.' Sect. 2.6.2.2.4.0, p. 364: 'The only published data in Kimaghama, Riantana, and Ndom are the notes collected by Drabbe (1949), an English abstract of which appeared in Boelaar…
new_statements.rule_in_words: According to Voorhoeve's reading of Drabbe's notes, word-stress position in Kimaghama is not predictable from word shape (lexical), with no recorded minimal pairs. The primary source, Drabbe 1949: 4 par. 8, gives no rule at all: 'Als we het nodig achten aan te geven welke lettergreep betoond wordt, dan doen we dat door een accent grave op de klinker van die syllabe te schrijven; tot welke soort de betoning in deze taal behoort, zullen we hier niet uitmaken' ('When we think it necessary to indicate which syllable is stressed, we do so by writing a grave accent on the vowel of that syllable; to what kind the accentuation in this language belongs we shall not determine here'). Drabbe's wordlist marks stress only sporadically, on initial, medial or final syllables in different words.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Voorhoeve: 'no cases of phonemic stress contrast have been recorded'; Riantana 'Suprasegmentals: as in Kimaghama'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Voorhoeve; inferred from Drabbe's accent-marked citation forms in a 469-item wordlist). Drabbe 1949: 4 par. 10 adds a phrase-level remark valid for all three languages: in N+N dependency compounds ('tree-fruit', 'pig-tail') 'de toon ligt in al die uitdrukkingen op het eerste of bepalende woord' (the accent lies on the first, determining word); in Ndom the same sequence with the opposite accent marks possession. Voorhoeve's statement is second-hand: he had no data beyond Drabbe 1949 ('The only published data.. are the notes collected by Drabbe (1949)').
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe 1949 describes the speech of informants from Kimaghama (Kimaam) village, the north-eastern dialect area; he notes at least two dialects. Usher (from Geurtjens 1933) distinguishes North Kimaghama (Teri Kalwasch) and South Kimaghama (Kaladdar); no separate Glottolog dialect codes seen. Voorhoeve 1975 misspells the name 'Kimaghana' once. Same statement applies to sister language Riantana (rian1263) per Voorhoeve ('Suprasegmentals: as in Kimaghama').

sources.note: Re-analyses Drabbe's 26-consonant/7-vowel inventory down to 13 C / 6 V; no statement on stress, but the cited Drabbe forms carry IPA stress marks copied from his grave accents (e.g. ˈmidœrœ, ˈmɛtɛ, ˈkuramu vs. miˈɛ, nœˈmɛ, tumaˈjɛ) - position varies word by word.
